title: What Should We Do About the "Forgotten Third"?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou follows up on her earlier criticism of expanded vocational education at 14 by answering the objection it provoked: if not new alternative pathways, what should schools do about the roughly third of students who fail to reach a grade 4 or above in GCSE English and maths? Her answer is deliberately unglamorous, get dramatically better at the existing academic pathway rather than build parallel tracks, on the grounds that literacy and numeracy have more labour-market value than allegedly vocational alternatives in an economy where unskilled labour has been automated away. She proposes an explicit 15-to-20-year target of moving 90-95 percent of students to a standard currently reached by only 60-65 percent, and grounds this ambition in the empirical existence of a small number of non-selective English schools already achieving 90-plus percent grade 4 pass rates. Christodoulou frames the debate as a choice between believing these results are scalable, her own 'Team Scalable' position, versus assuming a large cohort of students is simply incapable of the standard, and argues that critics proposing a return to an economy of local factory jobs for low-attaining school-leavers are chasing a political economy that Jim Callaghan already recognized as gone in his 1976 'Secret Garden' speech.
points: Christodoulou's core empirical claim is that GCSEs, despite being labeled 'academic,' often carry greater labour-market value than nominally 'vocational' 14-16 courses, because literacy and numeracy underpin nearly all modern jobs as unskilled labour has been automated away.

She sets a specific, falsifiable policy target rather than a vague aspiration: moving 90-95 percent of students to the standard currently reached by 60-65 percent within 15-20 years, anchored to PISA's level 2 'baseline proficiency for modern society' threshold, which about a fifth of English 15-year-olds currently miss.

Her argument leans on existence-proof evidence: a small number of non-selective English schools already achieve 90-plus percent GCSE grade 4 pass rates in English and maths, which she uses to counter the claim that a large cohort of students is structurally incapable of reaching that standard.

She directly rebuts the 'bring back local factory jobs' alternative policy pitch by noting that modern, reindustrialized manufacturing requires smaller, more highly skilled workforces than the 1950s factory economy nostalgia assumes.

Invoking Jim Callaghan's 1976 'Secret Garden' speech, she frames the 'large group of students can't reach the standard' position as fifty years behind an argument already settled: that rising school standards, not a return to an older economy, is the only viable response to structural economic change.
quotes: A lot of people accepted my point that vocational education in this country often conflates two groups of students: the 10-15% of students with an interest and aptitude in technical education, and the 30-40% who struggle to get grade 4+ GCSEs in English and maths.
GCSEs often get described as being "academic", but the irony is they often have greater labour market value than a lot of allegedly "vocational" 14-16 courses.
We should set an ambitious target that within 15-20 years, 90-95% of all students should reach the standard that is currently reached by only about 60-65%.
Over the last decade or so, the top 1% or so of non-selective schools in England have achieved some remarkable GCSE results that are well above the national average.

Is it going to mean lots more factories recreating mass employment for low-attaining school-leavers? I doubt it. Modern factories are highly automated and require smaller and more skilled workforces than in the past.
Callaghan realised in 1976 that the political economy of the 1950s was not coming back. I don't think anything has happened since then to prove him wrong.

Enough schools are achieving remarkable results now that we should be making some more systematic studies into what they have in common, what is replicable, and what the best methods of scaling their success would be.
